title: Episode 307: Henry VI: The Wars of the Roses, Margaret of Anjou, and the Cataclysm of Towton
description:
The heartbreaking forty-nine-year reign of King Henry VI, the holy and fragile sovereign whose inability to rule plunged England into the catastrophic Wars of the Roses. Inheriting the crowns of England and France as an eight-month-old baby, Henry grew into a deeply pious, gentle scholar who founded Eton College and King's College, Cambridge, but despised war and court politics. When the English empire in France collapsed in 1453, Henry suffered a devastating catatonic breakdown that rendered him completely unresponsive. In the power vacuum, his ferocious queen, Margaret of Anjou, waged war against Richard, Duke of York. The bloody feud culminated in 1461 at the Battle of Towton—the deadliest clash ever fought on English soil. Discover the saintly monarch whose weakness destroyed a dynasty.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series chronicles one of the most tragic figures in royal history: a monarch crowned in infancy over two kingdoms, whose saintly gentleness in a ruthless age sparked thirty years of civil slaughter known as the Wars of the Roses: King Henry VI. Here is George with the tragic fall of the House of Lancaster.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE INFANT KING OF TWO NATIONS: 1422 TO 1437
In December 1421, at Windsor Castle, Catherine of Valois gave birth to a healthy baby boy. When the joyous news reached Henry V in France, the king supposedly uttered a dark, chilling prophecy: 'Henry of Monmouth shall small time reign and much get, but Henry of Windsor shall long reign and lose all; God's will be done.' When Henry V died in August 1422, baby Henry was just eight months and twenty-six days old—the youngest person ever to inherit the English throne. Less than two months later, his French grandfather Charles VI died, making the infant theoretically King of France as well. England was governed during his minority by a regency council headed by his gifted uncles: John, Duke of Bedford, who maintained English mastery in France, and Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, who served as Protector of England. At age eight, Henry was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey in November 1429, and two years later in December 1431, he was crowned King of France at Notre-Dame in Paris. But the appearance of Joan of Arc and the resurgence of French national sentiment under the Dauphin Charles VII turned the tide of war irrevocably against the English garrisons. Baby Henry was crowned in England with a miniature gold crown specially fashioned for his tiny head, carried into the cathedral by his loving nurse Joan Astley. His childhood was cloistered and intensely monitored by Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick, who was authorized by the council to chastise the royal child when he misbehaved, instilling in Henry an anxious, submissive terror of conflict.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE PIOUS RECLUSE AND THE LOSS OF FRANCE: 1437 TO 1450
As Henry reached his majority in 1437, it became painfully apparent that he possessed none of his father's warrior spirit or iron will. Gentle, ascetic, and intensely religious, Henry hated violence, dressed in the simple dark robes of a monk, and was horrified by court profanity and bare décolletage. His enduring passion was education and architecture: he founded Eton College in 1440 to provide free education for poor boys, and King's College, Cambridge, in 1441, laying the foundation stone for the magnificent King's College Chapel with its breathtaking fan vaulting. But as a ruler, Henry was hopelessly incompetent, hopelessly naive, and easily manipulated by greedy courtiers led by William de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk. Desperate for peace with France at any price, Henry agreed in 1445 to marry Margaret of Anjou, a fierce, spirited fifteen-year-old French noblewoman, secretly agreeing to cede the vital strategic province of Maine to France without consulting Parliament. When the secret treaty leaked, English public opinion exploded in rage. Between 1449 and 1450, French armies overran Normandy in months; the English garrisons surrendered one after another, and in 1450, Cade's Rebellion of furious peasants and gentry marched on London, sacking the city before being suppressed. Henry was an architectural patron of transcendent genius: the chapel of King's College, Cambridge, with its vaulting by John Wastell, stands today as the supreme masterpiece of English Perpendicular Gothic. Yet Henry's excessive generosity was ruinous: he gave away crown lands, customs revenues, and castles to flattering courtiers, leaving the royal household so bankrupt that royal cooks had to beg food on credit to feed the king's table.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CATATONIC STUPOR AND THE DUKE OF YORK: 1453 TO 1454
In July 1453, the final English stronghold in Gascony fell at the Battle of Castillon, bringing a disastrous and permanent end to the Hundred Years' War; after three hundred years, England retained only the small enclave of Calais. When the catastrophic news reached King Henry at Clarendon Palace in August, the thirty-one-year-old monarch suffered a sudden, complete mental collapse, likely inherited from his French grandfather Charles VI. For seventeen agonizing months, Henry sat in a vegetative catatonic stupor: he could neither walk, stand, speak, nor recognize anyone, having to be fed and carried like an infant. In October 1453, Queen Margaret gave birth to their only child, Prince Edward of Westminster, but when the baby was placed in Henry's arms, the king showed not the slightest flicker of comprehension. With the throne paralyzed, the Royal Council appointed Richard, Duke of York—the wealthiest nobleman in the realm, descended from two sons of Edward III—as Protector of the Realm. York governed with remarkable efficiency and justice, reining in corrupt Lancastrian ministers. But on Christmas Day 1454, King Henry suddenly woke from his stupor as if from a long sleep, declaring himself at peace with God. Immediately, Queen Margaret reasserted her influence, stripped York of his offices, and banished him from court. Henry's catatonic breakdown in 1453 was so complete that contemporary chroniclers recorded he was 'as a man that had neither sight nor hearing, speech nor feeling.' The tragedy was compounded by the birth of his long-awaited son, Prince Edward: court gossips malicious of Queen Margaret circulated vicious rumors that the child was an adulterous bastard fathered by the Duke of Somerset, poisoning the dynastic waters.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: ST. ALBANS AND THE OUTBREAK OF THE WARS OF THE ROSES: 1455 TO 1460
Fearing imminent execution by Queen Margaret's faction, the Duke of York joined forces with the powerful Neville family, led by Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick—later known as 'Warwick the Kingmaker.' On May 22, 1455, the Yorkist lords intercepted the king's royal retinue at the walled town of St. Albans. When negotiations failed, Warwick's men broke through back gardens into the marketplace, catching the Lancastrians off guard. King Henry, sitting helplessly beneath his royal banner in the square while arrows flew around him, was grazed in the neck by an arrow before being escorted into a nearby tanner's cottage. The First Battle of St. Albans was small in scale, but monumental in consequence: key Lancastrian leaders, including the Duke of Somerset and the Earl of Northumberland, were killed, igniting a cycle of blood feuds that consumed the nobility. For five years, uneasy truces and theatrical reconciliations—such as the famous 'Loveday' procession of 1458 where rival lords walked hand-in-hand to St. Paul's Cathedral—failed to heal the breach. In July 1460, at the Battle of Northampton, Yorkist archers captured King Henry in his royal tent during a torrential downpour, while Margaret fled into the Welsh hills with her young son. The skirmish at St. Albans in 1455 shattered the sacred taboo against shedding noble blood on English soil in political disputes. The young sons of the slain Lancastrian lords—men like the new Duke of Somerset and Earl of Northumberland—vowed savage blood vengeance against the Yorkists, turning what had been a constitutional quarrel into an inescapable vendetta of mutual extermination.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BATTLE OF WAKEFIELD AND THE PAPER CROWN: 1460 TO 1461
Holding the captive king in London, the Duke of York took a fateful step: entering Westminster Hall, he walked directly to the empty throne and placed his hand upon the cushions, expecting the gathered lords to acclaim him king. Instead, an awkward, dead silence fell over the chamber. The English nobility was not ready to depose an anointed sovereign. A compromise was struck: the Act of Accord of October 1460 disinherited Henry's young son Edward, naming York and his heirs successors to the crown upon Henry's death. Queen Margaret, enraged that her son's royal birthright was stolen, raised a massive army in the north of England to rescue her husband. In December 1460, at the Battle of Wakefield in Yorkshire, Margaret's forces ambushed the Duke of York outside Sandal Castle. York was butchered on the field alongside his seventeen-year-old son, the Earl of Rutland. The Lancastrians severed York's head, placed a mocking crown of woven reeds and paper upon it, and impaled it above Micklegate Bar in York, sneering: 'So York may overlook the town of York!' Margaret's army marched south, looting towns and routing Warwick at the Second Battle of St. Albans, reuniting the queen with King Henry, who was found laughing and singing under a tree. The Act of Accord was an impossible compromise that satisfied no one: by disinheriting Prince Edward, it turned Queen Margaret into an unstoppable tigress fighting for her child's divine right. At Wakefield, the butchery of seventeen-year-old Edmund, Earl of Rutland, by Lord Clifford on Wakefield Bridge—where Clifford reportedly sneered, 'By God's blood, thy father slew mine, and so will I do thee!'—sealed the merciless nature of the war.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: BLOOD IN THE BLIZZARD: THE CATACLYSM OF TOWTON: MARCH 29, 1461
York's eighteen-year-old eldest son, Edward, Earl of March—a towering, charismatic warrior six-foot-four in height—immediately claimed his father's mantle. Proclaiming himself King Edward IV in London, young Edward marched north to finish the Lancastrian cause once and for all. On Palm Sunday, March 29, 1461, outside the village of Towton in Yorkshire, between fifty and sixty thousand Englishmen clashed in the middle of a blinding, howling snowstorm. It was the largest, longest, and bloodiest battle ever fought on British soil. The freezing north wind blew directly into the faces of the Lancastrians, blinding their archers and causing their arrows to fall forty yards short of the Yorkist lines, while Yorkist archers under Lord Fauconberg picked up the fallen arrows and fired them back with lethal effect. For ten uninterrupted hours, men hacked at each other in hand-to-hand combat amid drifts of red snow, the bodies piling so high that combatants had to climb over corpses to strike the enemy. When Warwick's reinforcements arrived late in the afternoon, the Lancastrian line shattered. Over twenty-eight thousand men—more than one percent of England's entire population—perished that day. The Cock Beck ran red with blood, and Henry, Margaret, and their son fled across the border into Scotland. The carnage of Towton was so horrific that local gravediggers took months to inter the fallen in massive trenches; contemporary letters described the snow falling through the branches of trees onto piles of corpses three deep. Edward IV, fighting on foot alongside his men with a battle-ax, proved his ferocious martial superiority, claiming the crown by right of conquest in the bloodiest trial by combat in English history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TOWER, THE READEPTION, AND MURDER IN THE NIGHT: 1465 TO 1471
For four years, Henry lived as a fugitive in the rugged hills of northern England and Scotland until he was betrayed by a monk in Lancashire in 1465. Brought to London with his legs tied beneath his horse's belly, Henry was imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he spent five years reading his Bible and praying. In 1470, an astonishing reversal occurred: Warwick the Kingmaker, having quarreled bitterly with Edward IV, allied with Queen Margaret and invaded England, forcing Edward to flee abroad. Dragging a bewildered, frail Henry from the Tower, Warwick restored him to the throne in an event known as the 'Readeption.' Dressed in a faded blue robe, Henry was paraded through London like a ghost. But the restoration lasted barely six months. In April 1471, Edward IV returned, slew Warwick at the Battle of Barnet in a heavy mist, and on May 4 routed Queen Margaret at Tewkesbury, where Henry's only son, Prince Edward, was slain. On the night of May 21, 1471, King Edward IV returned to London in triumph. That very night, inside the Wakefield Tower, forty-nine-year-old King Henry VI was brutally murdered while kneeling at his private oratory, his head bashed in with an iron mace or stabbed to death. The Yorkists announced he died of 'pure melancholy,' but no one was deceived. The pious founder of Eton was dead, and the direct Lancastrian line was extinguished forever. In the aftermath of Henry's murder in the Wakefield Tower, popular veneration for the gentle, saintly king spread like wildfire across England. Pilgrims flocked to his tomb at Chertsey Abbey and later Windsor Castle, reporting miraculous cures of blindness and fever; Henry VII would later lobby the Pope to canonize him as a formal saint of the Catholic Church, honoring the holy king who was too gentle for his violent world.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. If you enjoyed this chapter of Henry VI: The Wars of the Roses, Margaret of Anjou, and the Cataclysm of Towton, subscribe to the show, share it with a fellow history lover, and tune in next Tuesday for our next journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
